bonds.title: The station attendant
bonds.busy: I'm on the trains in the afternoon. Mornings and the middle of the day, I'm on this platform.

ranks.title: One track
ranks.invite: You keep looking up the line. Waiting for the train, or for the view? Got a moment of the {slot}?
talk: The Enoden is one track, both ways. The trains pass each other at a few places only: Enoshima, the signal stop at Minegahara just east of here, Inamuragasaki.
So every train waits for the one coming the other way. If one is late, they all are. Nobody here minds very much.
ranks.fact: The Enoden is single track for its whole 10 km between Fujisawa and Kamakura; trains pass each other only at a few stations and the Minegahara signal stop.

ask.q: Why not just lay a second track?

options.text: There's no room between the hill and the sea
options.reply: Look at it. The hill on one side, Route 134 and the sea on the other. Not a metre to spare.
Also true. But mostly: the hill on one side, the sea on the other. Not a metre to spare.

request.text: Ride the Enoden between two stations
request.ask: Have you been on it yet? One stop is enough. Sit on the sea side.

ranks.title: Nissaka
talk: This station is older than its name. It opened in 1903 as Nissaka, after the slope up the hill behind us.
It took the high school's name in 1953. The school is up that road, at the top of the slope.
ranks.fact: Kamakurakokomae Station opened in 1903 as Nissaka (日坂) and was renamed after Kamakura High School in 1953.

gives.name: The timetable by heart
gives.text: Lines: you know which way the trains wait

ranks.title: The old green ones
talk: See the pale green one with the cream band? Set 305. Built in 1960, the last of its series still running.
Two bodies on three bogies: the middle one is shared. That is why it bends like a caterpillar on the curves by Koshigoe.
ranks.fact: The Enoden's 300 series set 305 was built in 1960; like all Enoden stock it is a two-car articulated set, its two bodies sharing a middle bogie.

options.text: So it can take the tight curves
options.reply: Exactly. Some curves on this line are twenty-eight metres round. A long rigid car would never make it.
Fewer wheels does save money. But it's the curves: some are twenty-eight metres round.

request.text: Look down the hill road to the crossing
request.ask: Have you seen the crossing from up the hill? Everyone does it once. Go on.

ranks.title: Koshigoe's short platform
talk: At Koshigoe the platform is three cars long and the trains are four. So the last car stops over the crossing with its doors shut.
First-time riders panic. The announcement tells them to move forward. They never hear it.
ranks.fact: Koshigoe Station's platform holds three cars, so a four-car Enoden train keeps the doors of its last car shut there.

gives.name: A word from the platform
gives.text: 15% more for every job on this coast

ranks.title: Every fourteen minutes
talk: You know the line now. A train each way every fourteen minutes, from Fujisawa to Kamakura in thirty-seven.
People think it is slow. It is exactly as fast as the sea, the hill and the houses let it be.
ranks.fact: Since March 2023 the Enoden has run a train each way every 14 minutes; the whole line takes 37 minutes.

gives.name: Sato's coast
gives.text: Bearings, from someone who has watched it every day

bonds.title: The high school student
bonds.where: The crossing at the foot of the hill
bonds.busy: Class. I'm at the crossing before school and on my way home, weekdays.

ranks.title: The crossing
ranks.invite: You're not taking a picture? That's new. Got a minute of the {slot}?
talk: Every day there are people here with cameras, waiting for the train to cross with the sea behind it. From all over the world.
Our school is at the top of this hill. We walk down this road to the station every morning. It's just our road.
ranks.fact: Kamakura High School stands on the hill above the station that takes its name; its students walk down the road past the crossing to the platform.

ask.q: Does it get annoying, all the cameras?

options.text: It must make the road feel famous
options.reply: It does, a bit. My grandmother says nobody looked twice at it when she went here.
Ha. The neighbours would like that. Mostly people just need to stay off the road.

request.text: Take a picture of the crossing in the low light (photo mode, O)
request.ask: If you're going to take one, take it late in the day. The light goes gold over Enoshima.

ranks.title: Behind the line
talk: When the bell starts, stay behind the bar. The train comes round the curve faster than you think.
And watch the road. Cars come down the hill too, and they're looking at the sea, not at you.
ranks.fact: At a Japanese level crossing the bell and lamps start before the barrier falls; the barrier is down well before the train arrives.

ranks.title: The sea from class
talk: Our classrooms look at the sea. On winter mornings you can see Fuji over Enoshima.
Teachers say it's a distraction. The teachers look out of the window more than we do.
ranks.fact: On clear winter days Mount Fuji can be seen from Kamakura's coast, to the west beyond Enoshima.

request.text: Go out to the cape at Inamuragasaki and look west
request.ask: Have you been out to the cape? Go in the afternoon. On a good day it's the best view of Fuji on the whole coast.

ranks.title: Kites
talk: Never eat on the beach with your food out. The kites come down from behind and take it out of your hand.
They're big. Brown, a forked tail. One took a whole sandwich from my brother. He still talks about it.
ranks.fact: Black kites over Kamakura's beaches snatch food from people's hands; the city puts up signs warning beachgoers.

gives.name: Eat indoors
gives.text: Taste: where to eat out of the kites' reach

ranks.title: Graduation
talk: I graduate in March. I'll miss the walk down this hill more than anything inside the school.
Come back on a weekday morning. You'll see us all coming down, and the train arriving under us.
ranks.fact: The road from Kamakura High School falls steeply to the Enoden's crossing and Route 134 by the sea.

gives.name: The morning walk
gives.text: Light: the coast at every hour

bonds.title: The fisherman
bonds.busy: When the sea's up I don't go out, and nor should you. Find me at the harbour on a dry morning.

ranks.title: Shirasu
ranks.invite: You're up early. The boats are in. Want to see what came up this {slot}?
talk: Shirasu. Baby sardines, thin as a thread. We land them in the morning and they're on rice by lunch.
Raw, if the sea was kind and the boat was fast. Boiled, the rest of the time.
ranks.fact: Shirasu, the transparent young of sardines and anchovies, is the catch Koshigoe and the Shonan coast are known for; it is eaten raw (nama-shirasu) on the day it is landed.

ask.q: Why only raw on the day?

options.reply: By the afternoon it's gone cloudy. So you eat it here, or not at all.
It's the fish, not the tradition. By the afternoon it's gone cloudy.

request.text: Eat a bowl of shirasu at a counter in Koshigoe
request.ask: Have you eaten it yet? There's a counter on the street with the rails in it. Go.

ranks.title: The closed season
talk: In January and February the shirasu boats stay in. The bay is closed to us until the middle of March.
The day it opens, the whole street smells of it.
ranks.fact: Shirasu fishing in Sagami Bay is closed from 1 January to 10 March each year.

gives.name: In season
gives.text: Taste: you know when the fish is good

ranks.title: The train in the street
talk: Between here and Enoshima the train runs down the middle of the street. Shops on both sides, cars in front of it.
You learn to step aside without looking. The bell's enough.
ranks.fact: Between Koshigoe and Enoshima stations the Enoden runs down the middle of the street, sharing it with cars.

request.text: Walk the street with the rails in it to Koshigoe Station
request.ask: Walk the street once. Up the middle, with the rails. Mind the train.

ranks.title: Manpuku-ji
talk: Up behind the harbour there's an old temple, Manpuku-ji.
In 1185 Yoshitsune was stopped there by his own brother, and wrote him a letter begging to be let into Kamakura. He wasn't. Every school child knows the letter.
ranks.fact: At Manpuku-ji in Koshigoe, Minamoto no Yoshitsune wrote the Koshigoe Letter in 1185 to his brother Yoritomo, who had barred him from Kamakura.

gives.name: The harbour's goodwill
gives.text: 10% more for every job on this coast

ranks.title: Weather eye
talk: Forty years, and the sea still makes the decisions.
Wind from the south, swell on the reef, I stay in. You learn to read the water from the harbour wall before your coffee's cold.
ranks.fact: Koshigoe's fishing harbour lies at the west end of the coast, by Enoshima.

jobs.title: Which way from the crossing?
jobs.blurb: A tour group at the foot of the hill wants its bearings. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A tour group with matching hats

jobs.title: The crossing, the island and the cape
jobs.blurb: A travel magazine wants the crossing, Enoshima across the bay and the cape at Inamuragasaki. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: Kai flicks through them. "That one. With the train."

jobs.title: A cool box of shirasu
jobs.blurb: This morning's catch from Koshigoe harbour, along the coast to a kitchen by Shichirigahama's beach before it turns.
jobs.text: A cool box on a strap, cold to the touch. "Before noon, or it's soup."
jobs.done: "Still clear. Good. Sit, have a bowl."

jobs.title: A fare to the cape
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up a photographer at Koshigoe Station and take her along Route 134 to Inamuragasaki before the sun goes.
jobs.who: A photographer with a long lens
jobs.text: "The cape, please. Along the sea. I've got twenty minutes of light."

shops.name: Shirasu counter, Koshigoe しらす丼
shops.where: On the street with the rails in it
shops.hello: いらっしゃい! Raw or boiled? Raw's only till it runs out.

menu.name: Nama-shirasu don
menu.text: This morning's whitebait, raw and glassy, on rice with ginger and a little soy. Only on days the boats went out.

menu.name: Kamaage shirasu don
menu.text: Whitebait boiled in salted water as it comes off the boat: soft, white and mild, a mound of it on hot rice.

shops.name: Kitchen by the beach 浜の食堂
shops.hello: Hi! Sit by the window, you can watch the surf.

menu.name: Garlic shrimp plate
menu.text: Shrimp fried hard in garlic butter, with rice and a lemon. Eaten facing the sea, indoors, out of the kites' reach.

menu.name: Melon soda
menu.text: Bright green, with a scoop of vanilla on top. The colour of the Enoden, people say.

menu.name: Onigiri
menu.text: A triangle of rice round salmon, wrapped in seaweed you unpeel in three pulls. Eat it inside: the kites are watching.

menu.name: Bottled green tea
menu.text: Cold from the fridge, or hot from the warmer by the counter in winter.

events.title: The shirasu season opens
events.verb: Watch the first boats come in
events.text: Shirasu fishing in Sagami Bay opens on 11 March after two closed months, and the counters on Koshigoe's street serve it raw again.
lines: The first morning, the boats come in low in the water and the harbour is all gulls and shouting.
By lunch there's a queue at every counter on the street with the rails in it.

events.title: Fuji at sunset from the cape
events.native: 稲村ヶ崎の夕日と富士山
events.verb: Watch the sun go down by Fuji
events.text: In the clear air of late autumn and winter, the sun sets over Sagami Bay with Mount Fuji's outline beside Enoshima, seen best from the cape at Inamuragasaki.
lines: The mountain comes out of the haze a few minutes before the sun touches the sea, dark against the orange.
In 1333 Nitta Yoshisada threw his sword into the sea from this cape, the story goes, and the tide went out to let his army into Kamakura.
